title: Trading Systems: Lessons from The Matrix – Avoiding the Bugs
summary: Floating-point precision errors and async state management are hidden killers in trading systems; treating money as a float causes rounding errors that accumulate across trades, while unmanaged shared state in event-driven systems leads to race conditions and blown risk limits.
content:
The Quest Begins (The "Why")


Honestly, I still remember the first time I tried to build a tiny crypto‑trading bot. I was pumped, thinking I’d cracked the code to passive income while I slept. I wired up a quick Python script that pulled ticker data from an exchange, decided when to buy or sell based on a simple moving‑average crossover, and fired off market orders. The first few runs looked promising—my notebook showed a neat upward curve, and I felt like a superhero who’d just discovered a secret lair.  
Then reality hit. After a few hours, the bot started placing orders that were way off the price I expected. My balance dwindled, and the logs showed weird rounding errors: a 0.001 BTC order turned into 0.0009999999999 BTC, and the exchange rejected it for being below the minimum size. I spent three hours staring at floating‑point numbers, wondering why my “simple” math was betraying me. It felt like dodging barrels in Donkey Kong—every jump seemed fine until I missed the timing and fell into a pit.  
That frustration sparked a quest: I needed to understand the hidden traps that turn a promising trading system into a money‑leaking monster.  
The biggest eye‑opener? Money is not a float.  
When you represent currency with IEEE‑754 floating‑point numbers, you inherit binary rounding errors that are harmless for graphics or physics but deadly for accounting. A tiny epsilon can accumulate across thousands of trades, turning a profitable strategy into a loss‑maker, or worse, cause order rejections because the exchange enforces strict precision rules.  
The second revelation was about state and concurrency. Trading systems are inherently event‑driven: market data streams, order updates, and exchange responses arrive asynchronously. If you store shared state in a plain dict or list and update it from multiple callbacks without synchronization, you get race conditions—orders duplicated, positions mis‑calculated, and your risk limits blown sky‑high.

title: TouchGrass: a phone referee for outdoor games, with an open-weight Game Master
summary: TouchGrass is a multiplayer outdoor game referee app with a locally-running AI Game Master that proposes rule variations while game engine logic maintains authority; currently supports Tag and Hide & Seek for 2-4 players with additional games planned.
content:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 1: Touch Grass.
TouchGrass is a referee for outdoor games that lives on your phones, so nobody has to stay behind to keep score.
The idea is simple: everyone should be able to play instead of arguing about the rules, keeping score, or watching the clock. TouchGrass is designed to handle those jobs so friends, families, and youth groups can spend more time playing outside.
The project has a game engine, a multiplayer server, persistent game sessions, and an AI Game Master powered by an open weight model.
The Game Master can propose a twist for a round: a safe zone rule, a bonus challenge, or a little more time. But there is one important distinction: the AI proposes; the game engine decides.
The model never directly changes the game state. Its proposal must pass three checks implemented in ordinary code before it can be applied:
Gemma proposes
      ↓
Schema validation
      ↓
Game legality check
      ↓
Deterministic safety validation
      ↓
Game engine applies the event
      ↓
Players receive the update

If the model is slow, produces malformed output, proposes an illegal event, or is switched off, the game can continue without that AI event.
The project is intended for friends, families, and youth groups who want a reason to go to the park, and for anyone who has ever argued about whether a tag counted.
What works today: Tag and Hide & Seek are playable for 2–4 players, with three rounds and a named winner. Three other games Ice & Fire, Treasure Hunt, and Nature Challenge have their rules defined but are not playable yet. The website labels them as coming soon rather than pretending they are finished.
The browser-based gameplay client is not implemented yet. The game flow has been tested locally through the game server.
Live website: https://touchgrass-game-master.vercel.app/

title: Session Keys: the one Polymarket feature most traders ignore
summary: Polymarket traders often overlook Session Keys—a scoped signing feature that limits permissions and keeps master wallet keys offline, reducing account-takeover risk by separating trading keys from long-term storage keys.
content:
Most people sign every trade with their main wallet key. That's like carrying your house deed to the grocery store.
Polymarket's Session Keys exist to solve exactly this: a scoped signer with limited permissions, so your master key stays cold. At Coinbase, account-takeover incidents almost always started the same way — a hot key with too much power, phished once.
Three rules I follow:
Trading key != storage key. Never mix them.
The key that signs daily trades should hold only what you can afford to lose this week.
Hardware wallet for anything long-term. Browser extensions are for convenience, not custody.
None of this is exotic. It's boring hygiene — the kind that saves accounts.
(Full breakdown coming in my next post: how to set up scoped signers step by step.)
Not financial advice. Security is your responsibility.

title: Clock the First Fifteen Minutes
summary: The first 15 minutes of an AI coding session determine success—using a pre-session friction checklist (working directory verification, git status, branch permissions) filters out wrong setups before running prompts.
content:
The first fifteen minutes of an AI coding session are the product test, not a warm-up you can skip. If you cannot name the friction in that window, you should not trust the diff that follows it. I treat that opening as a drill, because chatter is an easy way to lose an afternoon without a diff. Have you ever closed a setup feeling productive, only to find that nothing reviewable landed in the tree?
Models keep getting louder in public, while the first edit on a real repository stays oddly quiet. I would run those minutes like a short drill, with a clock I own and a budget set before any prompt. A model can sound clever and still burn the window on a wrong directory or a silent authentication hop. The one fix I would bet on is not a smarter prompt, and it is not a longer context window either.
It is a friction ledger that refuses the first real edit until four cheap checks each have a timestamp. Think of that opening quarter hour as a kitchen in the tense minutes just before service begins. You can hire a famous chef and still miss the plate if the oven is cold and the ticket is blank. The coding assistant is the chef in this picture, and the oven is the working tree you meant to change.
The ticket is the task you can replay later, and the clock is the only judge that does not flatter you. I split the drill into four beats, and I give each beat a budget before I type a single prompt. Reach means I can talk to a model without guessing which door actually opened underneath me. Place means the process cwd is the repository I intend to change, not a parent folder I opened by habit.
Read means git status is clean enough that a later diff belongs to this session and not to yesterday. Touch means a throwaway branch can be created and deleted, which puts git state back where it started. If any beat blows the budget I chose, I stop and write down why before I try the next door. I'm Aman Kumar. I build an OpenAI-compatible gateway, and one of the most common support questions I see isn't about models at all. It's "streaming works in my terminal, but in the browser the whole answer shows up at once." The model is streaming fine. Something between your backend and the browser is holding the bytes.
This post is the setup I use for relaying a streamed chat completion from a Python backend to a web page, plus the specific places where buffering sneaks in.
Because the API key would ship to every visitor. Any key in front-end JavaScript is public. The normal pattern is:
The browser sends the user's message to your backend.
Your backend calls the LLM API with stream=True, using a key stored in an environment variable.
Your backend forwards each text chunk to the browser as it arrives.
Your backend also becomes the place to enforce per-user limits, log usage and pick the model, which you want anyway.

title: I Split the Score. Reach Was Never a Pass.
summary: Model evaluation methodology should split reach (API availability), contract (output format compliance), and check (correctness verification) into separate metrics rather than collapsing them into one pass/fail boolean.
content:
A free call that comes back with HTTP 200 is not a model that can do the job. I keep repeating that because a single pass rate keeps crawling back into the notes, wearing a lab coat. Reach, contract, and check are three different arguments. Glue them into one boolean and you will praise a host for being awake, or blame a model for a timeout it never saw.
You know the Tuesday demo. Same prompt, Wednesday, and the body is empty, or half an object, or a charming paragraph that fails the checker you trusted last month. Which piece actually broke? If you stored one bit, you cannot say. You graded a smoothie and called it fruit.
This is a protocol, not a scoreboard from a run I am about to invent. No latency trophy. No win rate. Those numbers belong to a log you produce yourself. What I will hand you is the split, a harness, and a rule for which column is allowed to speak.
Picture a clinic that publishes one word, healthy. Blood pressure, whether the patient showed up, and whether the vial was labeled all collapse into that word. A missed appointment looks like a bad heart. A mislabeled vial looks like a no-show. You would fire that clinic. Why do we publish model evals that way?
Free model access makes the blend worse, not kinder. A free server is a second moving part. It can refuse, queue, reset, or idle-timeout while the weights sit there innocent. A free model can also be perfectly reachable and still emit prose where your tool wanted an object. Score only the final checker and both failures wear the same red mark. Then the postmortem becomes a vibe.
I am not stating a quota, a model list, a box size, or a promise that any free tier stays free next week. Those facts rot on contact. If a vendor page is your source, read it the day you run, and paste that URL into the run record. Do not borrow a sentence from a blog as a spec.

title: JWT Authentication Explained: Theory, Security, and a Complete Node.js & Express Example
summary: JWT tokens securely transmit claims using header-payload-signature format; this guide covers authentication vs. authorization, token structure, implementation in Node.js/Express, and security best practices for token storage.

You will find JWT in:

React applications
Node.js APIs
Mobile applications
Microservices

API gateways

But JWT is often misunderstood.
Many developers know how to write:
jwt.sign(...)

and:
jwt.verify(...)

This article goes beyond simply generating a token.
We will understand JWT from the ground up and build a complete authentication flow using Node.js, Express, TypeScript, and MongoDB-style concepts.
Before discussing JWT, we need to understand two fundamental concepts.
Authentication answers:
Who are you?
For example:
User → Email + Password
        ↓
     Server
        ↓
  Is the user valid?
        ↓
       Yes

The server identifies the user.
Authorization answers:
What are you allowed to do?
For example:
User
 ├── Read products       ✅
 ├── Create products     ❌
 ├── Delete products     ❌
 └── Manage users        ❌

Authentication comes first.
Authorization comes after authentication.
JWT stands for:
JSON Web Token
It is a compact token format used to securely transmit claims between parties.

HEADER.PAYLOAD.SIGNATURE

title: AVIF to JPG vs PNG: Which Image Format Should You Choose?
summary: The article compares three image formats—AVIF, JPG, and PNG—explaining their trade-offs: AVIF offers efficient compression for modern websites, JPG provides broad compatibility for photographs, and PNG preserves details and transparency for graphics. Choosing the right format depends on specific needs like compatibility, file size, transparency requirements, and intended use case.
content:
AVIF, JPG, and PNG are popular image formats, but each has different strengths depending on how you plan to use an image. AVIF offers efficient compression and good visual quality, JPG is widely supported and works well for photographs, and PNG is known for preserving image details without lossy compression. Understanding these differences can help you choose the right format for your website, photos, documents, or other everyday tasks.
JPG is often a practical choice when you need an image that works across different devices, applications, and online platforms. It uses lossy compression to reduce file size, making it suitable for photographs, email attachments, and general image sharing. Converting AVIF to JPG can be helpful when a website or application does not support AVIF files. However, the conversion may remove some image information, so choosing an appropriate quality setting is important.
PNG is a better option when you need transparency or want to preserve sharp details without introducing additional lossy compression. It is commonly used for logos, icons, screenshots, diagrams, and graphics with text or clear edges. Unlike standard JPG images, PNG supports transparent backgrounds, which makes it useful for placing graphics over different colors or images. However, PNG files can be larger than JPG files, especially when they contain detailed photographs.
AVIF can be a strong choice for modern websites because it can deliver good visual quality at relatively small file sizes. Smaller images can help reduce bandwidth usage and improve page loading performance. AVIF also supports features such as transparency, but compatibility may vary across older software and some platforms. If your website supports AVIF, keeping images in this format may be beneficial; if a service requires JPG or PNG, converting the image can make it easier to use.

title: Profit Factor vs Win Rate for Trading Bots
summary: While win rate measures the percentage of profitable trades, profit factor—the ratio of gross profit to gross loss—is a more reliable metric for evaluating trading bot performance. Neither metric alone determines success, but together with expectancy calculations, they provide insight into whether a trading strategy is truly profitable or just lucky.
content:
Profit factor is usually the more useful of the two, because it measures whether a bot's wins are bigger than its losses. Win rate only tells you how often it wins. Neither number is enough alone, though. A bot can win 80% of its trades and still lose money, and a bot that wins 35% of the time can come out ahead. This guide explains both metrics, how they relate, and how to use them together without fooling yourself.
Win rate is the share of closed trades that ended in profit:
Win rate = winning trades ÷ total trades
It is easy to understand and easy to market, which is why bot sellers love to quote it. But it ignores two things that decide whether a strategy makes or loses money:
How big the wins are compared with the losses
How much each trade costs in fees, funding and slippage
A high win rate often comes from taking profit quickly and letting losers run. That produces lots of small wins and a few large losses. The equity curve looks smooth for weeks, then one bad trade wipes out a month of gains.
Profit factor compares the money made on winning trades with the money lost on losing trades:
Profit factor = gross profit ÷ gross loss
How to read it:
Below 1.0: the bot lost money over the sample
Exactly 1.0: break-even before anything else goes wrong
Above 1.0: winners outweighed losers over the sample
Profit factor captures both how often a bot wins and by how much. That makes it a better first summary than win rate. It still has weaknesses, which we cover below.
The cleanest way to connect the two metrics is expectancy, the average result per trade:
Expectancy = (win rate × average win) − (loss rate × average loss)
From it you can work out the break-even win rate for any payoff profile:
Break-even win rate = average loss ÷ (average win + average loss)
This one formula answers most "is this win rate good?" questions. A 70% win rate is excellent if the average loss equals the average win. It is a losing system if the average loss is five times the average win.

title: How Many Trades Does a Backtest Need? A Practical Guide
summary: Backtests with under 30 trades provide minimal information, around 100 trades begin to show meaningful signals, and several hundred trades across different market conditions produce reliable results. The uncertainty around a bot's average return shrinks with the square root of trade count, meaning traders need four times more trades to halve their uncertainty.
content:
There is no single magic number. As a rough guide, under 30 trades tells you almost nothing, around 100 starts to be informative, and several hundred trades across different market conditions is where a backtest becomes hard to dismiss. The number you actually need depends on how big the bot's average edge is compared with how noisy its individual trades are. This guide shows you how to work that out.
Every backtest is a small sample of a strategy's possible outcomes. If you flip a fair coin 10 times, getting 7 heads is not unusual. Trading results work the same way. A bot with zero real edge can produce a beautiful equity curve over 20 or 40 trades purely by luck.
The question a backtest should answer is not "did it make money?" but "how likely is it that this result came from luck?" Trade count is the main thing that shrinks luck's influence.
The uncertainty around a bot's average result per trade shrinks with the square root of the number of trades. That has an uncomfortable consequence:
To halve your uncertainty, you need 4x the trades.
To cut it to a third, you need 9x the trades.
This is why 50 trades feels like a lot but usually isn't.
These are rules of thumb, not laws. Treat them as a starting point:
Under 30 trades: Anecdote. Useful for spotting obvious bugs, not for judging an edge.
30–100 trades: Early signal. You can rule out strategies that are clearly broken, but a profitable-looking result can still easily be noise.
100–300 trades: Informative, if trades are reasonably independent and the edge per trade is not tiny.
300+ trades across several market regimes: Strong enough to take seriously, provided you didn't test hundreds of variants to find it.
Measure each trade in R (profit or loss divided by the amount risked). A bot averaging +0.5R per trade with consistent outcomes needs far fewer trades to prove itself than one averaging +0.05R with wild swings. Small edges need big samples.

title: Why AI Agents Need Blockchain Runtime Controls
summary: As AI agents move beyond text generation to executing real-world actions like financial transactions, there's a need for external runtime controls to ensure accountability and prevent harm. Blockchain primitives can provide cryptographic identities, irrefutable mandates, enforceable boundaries, and tamper-proof audit trails that keep probabilistic AI systems within defined guardrails.
content:
AI agents have stopped just answering questions. They move money, sign contracts, change production systems and act on customer accounts. That shift creates a problem nobody designed for: a probabilistic model is now triggering deterministic, irreversible actions.
An LLM can be wrong, manipulated by a prompt injection, or simply drift. When its output was a paragraph of text, that was a quality problem. When its output is a wire transfer, it's a liability problem.
Most teams try to solve this inside the model: better prompts, filters, fine-tuning. That helps, but it asks the same probabilistic system to police itself. What's missing is a layer outside the model that decides what the agent is allowed to do, and proves afterwards what it actually did.
That's what runtime controls are. At AtBash we build them on blockchain primitives, because they give you four things that are hard to fake:
Cryptographic identities. Every agent has a verifiable identity, so you always know which agent acted and on whose behalf.
Irrefutable mandates. What an agent is allowed to do (limits, counterparties, scopes) is signed and anchored, not buried in a prompt that can be talked around.
Enforceable red lines. Actions outside the mandate are blocked at execution time, regardless of what the model "decided".
Tamper-proof audit trails. Every action is recorded in a way no one can quietly edit later: not the agent, not the vendor, not an insider. When a regulator, auditor or insurer asks "prove it", you can.
The result: agents become controllable and accountable, which is what lets enterprises move them from pilots into production.
This isn't theoretical. Enterprises already pay for AtBash today, including two banks, and we recently joined NVIDIA Inception.
If you're deploying agents that touch money, data or infrastructure, I'd love to compare notes.
Yosef, Founder, AtBash

Stop Uploading Sensitive PDFs to Random Websites


Every time you upload a contract, medical record, or financial statement to a "free PDF tool" site, you're trusting a stranger's server with your most sensitive documents.
Here's what actually happens on most free PDF sites:
Your file uploads to their server
It sits there (for how long? who knows)
It gets processed, maybe logged, maybe backed up
You hope they delete it
Modern browsers can do everything a server can for PDF work:
pdf.js extracts text from any PDF
pdf-lib merges, splits, rotates, edits
Tesseract.js does OCR on scanned pages
Canvas API renders pages to images
None of this needs a server. Your file never leaves your device.

Merge, split, compress, convert, edit, sign
11 AI tools (summarizer, MCQ generator, chat with PDF, contract checker)
Works offline as a PWA after first load
The only exception: AI tools send extracted text (not your file) to the AI. Everything else is 100% local.
Open DevTools → Network tab → upload a file → if you see your file in an upload request, it's going to their server. Check if it works offline (airplane mode) — if yes, it's truly client-side. Read the privacy policy — vague = red flag.
If a free tool needs your file on their server to do something your browser can do alone, find another tool.

summary: Path-scoped rules in repositories clarify which coding guidelines apply to specific directories, making constraints more relevant and easier to follow than overwhelming project-wide rules. By using frontmatter to define applicable file globs, developers receive contextually appropriate guidance without unrelated instructions cluttering their workflow.
content:
A Path-Scoped Rule Is a Matching Contract, Not Just a Note


A rule that applies everywhere is easy to write and expensive to live with.
Projects accumulate instructions: validate API input, preserve migration compatibility, write release notes, keep documentation examples current. Those instructions are all useful. They are not all relevant while an agent is editing the same file.
APC gives this distinction a portable shape. Repository-wide expectations belong in AGENTS.md. A rule that only matters for a slice of the tree belongs in .apc/rules/ with frontmatter that says where it applies. The thesis is simple: a path-scoped rule is a matching contract. Its glob is part of its meaning.
Imagine a repository with an API and a documentation site. The API needs request-boundary validation and careful compatibility handling. Documentation pages need accurate examples, but do not need a warning about route validation on every edit.
Put the API-specific instruction in a rule file such as .apc/rules/backend.mdc:
---
description: "Backend API rules"
globs:
  - "src/api/**/*.ts"
alwaysApply: false
---

- Validate request input at the route boundary.
- Keep public API compatibility during migrations.

The file holds two different facts. The Markdown body explains what to do. The frontmatter explains when the instruction matters. Removing either half changes the contract.
alwaysApply: false matters


alwaysApply: false expresses a useful restraint: do not make this a project-wide command. A task that changes src/api/orders.ts should receive backend rules. A task that updates docs/getting-started.mdx should not have to treat those rules as the primary context.
This is not an attempt to hide important constraints. It is how you make constraints easier to follow. A relevant, narrow rule is more likely to be noticed and less likely to be diluted among unrelated instructions.

content:
Coder answered 15 fingerprints: development environments that hold repository and cloud credentials


Coder provisions development environments from templates and gives the people who own them a shell inside that environment. It is a platform for creating workspaces, and it necessarily holds the keys that those workspaces need in order to be useful.
The query app="Coder" returned 15 matches on 2026-10-06 with the scope set to all asset types. The result is an application fingerprint, so it describes services whose banner names the product.
Provisioning a workspace means reaching a compute provider, cloning repositories and, in most setups, authenticating the developer who asked for it. The platform therefore stores provider credentials, template definitions and, through single sign-on, the identity of each user. It also brokers the tokens that a workspace uses to reach the internal systems it was created for.
The product implements user roles, workspace ownership and template permissions, and it supports external identity providers. Authentication is enforced for the interface by default. The open questions in a given deployment are which provider is configured, whether registration is open, and how broad the template permissions are. A template that provisions a privileged container with a mounted provider credential decides the blast radius of every workspace built from it.
Fifteen fingerprints is a small population, and it matches the profile of a platform that organisations run internally. Nothing in the count says that any of those instances is misconfigured. What it says is that a workspace platform, which by design holds credentials with which to reach other systems, is occasionally reachable, and that the design intent of such a platform is worth understanding before it is exposed.

title: GEO is the second layer of SEO: why your brand is missing from AI answers
summary: As AI systems answer queries by selecting sources rather than listing links, a new visibility layer called GEO determines whether brands appear in AI responses. Organizations must publish verifiable business facts—legal name, business scope, and contact information—rather than brand narratives for AI engines to cite them.
content:
GEO is the second layer of SEO — why your brand does not appear in AI answers


If you sell to overseas buyers, you have probably noticed something odd. Your website ranks on page one for a keyword, and the brand appears in an AI answer — but not always. Sometimes you are simply absent, and no amount of traditional SEO fixes it.
This is not a ranking problem. It is a different problem.
Layer 1 — SEO. You optimized for a crawler. You earned positions. That still works, and it is not going away.
Layer 2 — GEO. An AI engine answers a question by selecting and composing sources. It does not show a list of blue links. So the question changes from "what is my rank?" to "am I one of the sources this engine chose to cite?"
A page can rank #1 and still be skipped. The engine picked four other sources — probably the ones that looked most verifiable.
Before an AI engine recommends a company, it checks whether that company exists as a real organization. In practice it looks for three things:
Legal name — the registered entity, not just a brand name
Business scope — what you actually do, stated concretely
Reachable contacts — a physical address, a working email, a phone number
Publish those three and you have laid the baseline. Fail them and you are not penalized, exactly — you are simply skipped, which reads the same way from the outside.
Most exporters publish none of them. Their "About" page is a founder's story, not a set of checkable facts.
We operate airport and high-speed-rail advertising media alongside an AI content practice, so we get to test our own advice. A few observations from shipping this:
Facts beat adjectives. "Leading provider" is unfalsifiable and gets ignored. "Unified Social Credit Code 91500103686203135J, registered at Room 52, 25F, No.1 Huasheng Road, Yuzhong District, Chongqing" is checkable. Engines prefer checkable.

title: Little's Law: The One Formula That Tells You When Your System Will Break
summary: Little's Law (L = λ × W) from queueing theory mathematically predicts when systems fail under load by calculating average concurrent items based on arrival rate and processing time. This formula reveals the nonlinear cliff where slightly-above-normal traffic causes catastrophic degradation and queue collapse.
content:
Little's Law: The One Formula That Tells You When Your System Will Break


Most capacity planning advice is vibes: "add more servers," "it'll scale." There's a better way. One equation from queueing theory — Little's Law — lets you predict exactly when your system tips from "handling it" into "meltdown." It fits on a napkin, and it has saved more launches than any autoscaling policy ever will.
L = λ × W
L = average number of items in the system (requests being processed, jobs in a queue, users on your servers)
λ (lambda) = average arrival rate (requests per second)
W = average time each item spends in the system (seconds)
That's it. If 100 requests arrive per second and each takes 0.5 seconds to process, you have on average 50 requests in flight at any moment. Your system must be able to hold 50 concurrent requests — or the queue grows forever.
Benchmarks tell you what your server can do under ideal conditions. Little's Law tells you what will happen under your actual traffic. The difference is the queue. When arrivals outpace service even slightly, the queue doesn't grow slightly — it grows without bound. That's the cliff every outage postmortem describes: "traffic was only 20% above normal."
Let's make it concrete. Your API handles checkout requests:
Arrival rate (λ): 40 requests/second at peak
Average processing time (W): 0.8 seconds (payment gateway calls are slow)
Average concurrent requests (L): 40 × 0.8 = 32



Your server pool must comfortably handle 32 concurrent checkouts. If your connection pool caps at 25, you don't get "slightly slower checkouts" — you get timeouts, retries, and a retry storm that doubles your arrival rate. Now λ is 80, L wants to be 64, and you're down.
You don't need a PhD. You need three measurements:
Peak arrival rate — not average, peak. Check your last traffic spike, then add 50% headroom. Averages lie; peaks kill.

title: React Native SMS OTP Recovery: Node.js Backend Autofill and Abuse Controls
summary: SMS OTP recovery must be implemented server-side with single-use challenges, short expiry windows, and strict rate limiting by account and device. Monitoring recovery funnel transitions reveals infrastructure problems early; autofill is a usability feature but not proof of possession and cannot replace server-side validation.
content:
For a React Native mobile app, an SMS OTP login recovery API belongs on the backend. A server-owned, single-use challenge carries a short expiry and an attempt limit. The resend path must not extend the challenge deadline. The app should request and submit codes; it should never decide whether a code is valid, how many attempts remain, or when another message may be sent.
Short answer: treat SMS OTP as an administrator account-recovery ceremony, not as a messaging feature. Bind each challenge to the recovery transaction, store only a keyed digest of the code, make verification atomic, and rate-limit by account, destination, device, and network. Autofill is a usability hint. It is not proof of possession.
The page says “administrator recovery completion rate below SLO.” On-call sees requests, sends, deliveries where the carrier exposes them, verification attempts, and successful recoveries split by country and carrier. A logistics SaaS cannot let a dispatcher remain locked out during an overnight exception, but lowering every control during an incident turns an availability problem into an account-takeover problem.
A page on raw SMS send errors fires too late and often points at the wrong layer. The earlier signal is the recovery funnel: accepted challenge requests are rising, but verified challenges are not. Instrument each state transition with a low-cardinality reason such as expired, attempts_exhausted, superseded, send_rejected, or verified; keep phone numbers, codes, and free-form carrier text out of metric labels and logs. Then inspect the shape before changing policy: a broad increase in send_rejected points toward transport or destination quality, a concentration of expired outcomes may indicate late arrival, and a jump in superseded challenges usually means the resend experience deserves attention. title: My Free Sample Said 11 Chapters on the Cover and 15 at the End
summary: An autonomous agent fixed one chapter count reference in a PDF but missed another identical reference in the same file, creating inconsistency where the cover said 11 chapters and the back matter said 15. Comprehensive pattern-matching tests across the entire document caught this remaining discrepancy that single-location tests had missed.
content:
A field note from the autonomous Claude Code agent I run every day on one Windows PC. The numbers come from its own ledgers, not from memory.
Free to read first: a PDF sample of the book behind this setup — its first 3 chapters: https://dbsoul.gumroad.com/l/autonomous-ai-agents-claude-code-free-sample
My book has a free English sample: the first three chapters as a PDF. My agent rebuilt it to fix two problems, and the independent auditor found a third problem that the fix had left behind.
The line under the sample's cover title said "3 chapters + 0 ready-to-use templates". The full book has 4 templates. The cover code counted only the manuscript files that are inside the sample, and the sample has no templates, so the count was 0.
The agent changed the line to "Free sample · chapters 1–3 of 11". The 11 comes from the function that counts the book's chapters, not from the files in the sample. A test checks the sample cover, and another test checks that the full book's cover did not change.
The last page of the same PDF tells the reader what the rest of the book contains. It said "This sample is the first 3 chapters of 15."
That 15 came from a different count: the number of manuscript files in the full book. That is 11 chapters plus 4 template files. So after the fix, one PDF gave two different totals: 11 on the cover and 15 at the end.
The agent had fixed one line that stated the chapter count. It did not search the same file for the other lines that state it. The test it added also looked only at the cover.
The auditor caught the two totals and failed the work.
The last page now uses the same chapter-count function as the cover.
The new test takes the whole sample, pulls out every "of N" chapter total with a regular expression, and requires that set to be exactly one number: the chapter count. Before the fix, the test failed with {11, 15} == {11}. That is the bug in one line: two totals where there should be one.

title: The Best Writing Platform Isn’t One Platform: A Small Audience-Growth Experiment
summary: Rather than optimizing for a single algorithm, this writing audience experiment tests a distributed multi-platform approach where each platform serves a specific function: DEV.to for discovery, Substack for retention, Medium for search reach, and X for conversation. Distribution and ownership are separated concerns requiring different strategies.
content:
Discovery, reader relationships, and income are different jobs. Here’s the evidence-led system I’m testing instead of chasing one algorithm.
A post can reach strangers and still leave you with no direct way to reach them again. An email list can create a permission-based relationship and still sit unread if nobody discovers it. Distribution and ownership are different jobs.
Open Reader Lab is an AI-assisted, source-linked experiment in building a useful writing audience from zero. This is the first long-form entry. There are no growth results yet: I’m documenting the decisions and measuring what happens, not presenting a case study that hasn’t happened.
1. Discovery: help the right new readers encounter useful work. Feeds, search, recommendations, and community discussions can help, but none guarantees distribution.
2. Conversion: make the next step clear when someone finds a post. A follow, an email signup, or a return visit is more meaningful than an impression alone.
3. Retention: give readers a reason to come back. A consistent promise and a recognizable format matter more than posting everywhere without a plan.
4. Revenue: earn only after readers find enough value to pay, buy, recommend, or hire. Eligibility gates, payment availability, fees, and trust matter more than a payout headline.

title: I Built TubeZap — Get Full YouTube Transcripts in Seconds, Free Forever
summary: TubeZap is a free web tool that extracts YouTube transcripts without signup or API keys, solving the friction of manually copying captions from YouTube's UI. Features include timestamped text, PDF/TXT export, in-transcript search, and support for multiple YouTube URL formats across any language with auto-generated captions.
content:
I keep running into the same annoyance: there's a 45-minute tutorial on YouTube with exactly one useful answer buried inside it, and the only way to get it is to scrub through the whole thing at 2x speed. Auto-generated captions exist, but YouTube buries them behind menus and makes them nearly impossible to copy cleanly. I wanted a paste-link-get-text tool that just works.
So I built TubeZap — a free YouTube transcript generator. Paste any YouTube link and you get the full transcript in seconds, with or without timestamps. No signup, no extension, no API key. Free forever.
How it works is deliberately boring: you paste a YouTube URL, TubeZap fetches the video's caption data, and hands you back clean text. It supports youtube.com, youtu.be, Shorts, and mobile links — basically any public video with captions, which is the vast majority of YouTube in every language.
The features I actually use myself:
Timestamps on every line — clickable, so you can jump straight to that moment in the video.
Download as TXT or PDF — clean files with the video details included.
Search inside the transcript — find any word or phrase, see the match count, jump to highlighted results.
Multiple copy formats — with timestamps, as plain text, or as flowing paragraphs. Choose what you need.
Video info up top — title, channel, duration, and thumbnail, so you always know what you're reading.
I built this because my own workflow needed it. I'm constantly turning videos into notes, quotes for posts, and references for projects. Copy-pasting from YouTube's caption panel was a weekly tax on my time, and the paid "YouTube to text" tools charge for something that shouldn't cost anything. The caption data is already there — extracting it shouldn't need an account or a credit card.

title: Show HN: WallHop – 12ft.io is gone, so I built a replacement
summary: WallHop is a free paywall bypass tool that combines multiple bypass techniques with fallback to archive.is to help users access paywalled articles without signup or installation. The tool supports iOS shortcuts, works on Medium member-only posts, and offers bookmarklet and API endpoints for greater accessibility.
content:
Hi HN, I'm Josh. WallHop is a free paywall bypass: paste an article URL (or prefix any URL with wallhop.io/) and you get the readable article without the paywall popup, ads or clutter. No signup, no extension.
I built it after 12ft.io went away. The News Media Alliance took it down in July 2025 and I missed having something I could hit from my phone.
How it works: it started as a fork of everywall/ladder (GPL-3.0) and I've modified it heavily since. Instead of relying on one trick, it chains several bypass methods per request and falls back to archive.is when they all fail, so one site blocking one technique doesn't break it.
Things that might be interesting:
- iOS Shortcut: on iPhone, tap Share > WallHop from any article in Safari or another app. This is how I use it 95% of the time.
- It works on Medium member-only posts, which 12ft never handled.
- Bookmarklet for desktop, plus /raw/ and /api/ endpoints if you want to script it.
I've tested it against most major news outlets and a bunch of local papers. It won't work everywhere. There are SOME server-side paywalls that are out of reach, and I'd rather say that up front. If you find a site that breaks, I'd love the link, and I can likely figure out a way to bypass it!
